meta.blurb: Marta delivers parcels, worries about money, and has no plan. Over ten years she builds one on a single page: know your numbers, keep a gap, clear debt, hold a cushion, and let one plain fund grow. Simple enough to start tonight.
meta.bible: Marta: a parcel delivery driver aged thirty-eight at the start, practical and a little tired of money worry. Kofi: her younger brother, a student with many questions. Dev: Marta's partner, a school cook, who joins the plan in the second half. The plan: Marta writes it on one page and keeps it for ten years. All money amounts are plain numbers with no currency. The examples (yearly costs of 24,000, a pile of about 600,000) are imagined illustrations, not promises. Key terms: wealth, income, assets, debt, net worth, savings rate, emergency cushion, broad fund, rule of thumb, automate, inflation, withdrawal. A rule of thumb that a pile of about twenty-five times yearly costs may support spending is described as a guide only and not a guarantee. Markets can fall and recover; no returns are promised. Tax and employer plans differ by country. Voice: calm, plain, encouraging and honest. The final beat says this is general information and not financial advice.

B1B2: Marta is thirty-eight, and she delivers parcels all day in a small white van. She earns a steady wage, but she has no plan for her money, and at night she lies awake and worries.
Her younger brother Kofi is studying at university, and he asks her a simple question over dinner. What does it really mean to be wealthy, and how do you get there?
They work it out together, and the answer surprises them. Wealth is not what you earn or what you show, but what you own and keep after you have paid what you owe.
Kofi draws a picture with three wheels that turn together. The first wheel is earning, the second is keeping, and the third is growing what you have kept.
Marta decides that her plan must fit on a single page, with only a few clear steps. If it is too complicated, she knows that she will never follow it.
Step one is to know all of her numbers, as clearly as she can. Marta spreads out her bills, her bank statement and her loan letter, and she writes down what she earns, spends, owns and owes.
Subtracting what she owes from what she owns, Marta finds her net worth. It is small, and for a moment it embarrasses her, but it is her honest starting point.
Next, Marta adds up what her life costs each month and multiplies the total by twelve. This yearly figure will become the centre of her whole plan.
Step two is to spend less than she earns. The gap between the money coming in and the money going out is the engine that powers the whole plan.
Marta notices that three costs are far bigger than all the others: housing, transport and food. These three will matter much more than any small daily saving.
Marta and her partner Dev decide to move to a smaller, cheaper flat that is closer to her work. One decision cuts her biggest cost, and it saves more than a hundred small ones.
Step three is to pay off any debt that charges high interest. Marta has a credit card with a large balance, and every month the interest takes a bite out of her plan.
After nine months of steady payments, the credit card is finally clear, and Marta feels as light as a feather. She decides that only cheap, useful debt, such as a fair loan, may be kept.
Step four is a cushion that she can use for emergencies. Marta decides to save enough to cover a few months of her costs, so that a surprise will never again become a debt.
Marta keeps her cushion in a safe account that she can reach quickly. It is kept apart from her investments, because money for emergencies should never depend on the market.
Step five is to grow the rest of her money over many years. Marta chooses one broad, low-cost fund that holds hundreds of companies, so her savings are spread widely.
Marta decides that one fund is better than a dozen, because every extra choice is another chance for a mistake. One fund also keeps her costs low and her thinking clear.
Kofi tells Marta to ask anyone who sells her a financial product how they are paid. Complicated products are often the ones that earn the seller the most money.
Over long periods, markets have tended to rise, but the road has been bumpy. There have been sharp falls along the way, and nobody can say when the next one will come.
Marta writes a rule on a card and tapes it to the fridge. When prices fall, she will not sell in a panic, and she will not check her fund every day.
Step six is to make everything automatic, so that nothing depends on her memory. On the day after payday, money moves into her cushion and her fund without Marta lifting a finger.
Kofi explains that the share of income that you save is the most powerful lever. The more you save, the sooner you will not need to work for money.
How big a pile of money will Marta need, in the end, to feel free? Some planners use a rule of thumb: about twenty-five times her yearly costs, though this is only a rough guide and not a promise.
Suppose that her life costs 24,000 a year, as an imagined example. Twenty-five times that figure is about 600,000, and this is the rough target that she might work toward over the years.
Marta sees that lowering her yearly costs by 1,000 cuts the target by about 25,000. It also frees more money to save, so she gains twice.
Saving is only half of the plan, so Marta also looks for ways to earn more. She signs up for a night course that could help her become a transport manager.
Many countries have special accounts that protect savings from some tax, and some employers add money too. Marta checks the rules in her country, and she uses what she finds.
One year after she wrote her plan, Marta checks every line of her page. Her cushion is full, her card balance is gone, and the first small growth has appeared in her fund.
In the second year, her old van breaks down and needs an expensive repair. Because she has a cushion, she pays the bill without borrowing and without losing a night's sleep.
In her third year, markets fall sharply, and the value of her fund drops by about a fifth. Marta reads the card on her fridge, takes a deep breath, and does nothing at all.
After a while, prices recover, although nobody could have said when that would happen. Marta learns that patience, and not cleverness, was her real job.
Kofi's friend put most of his savings into a fashionable new idea, and he lost a large part of it. Marta feels sorry for him, and she is glad that her plan is plain.

Marta and Dev think about buying a home of their own after a few years. Neither buying nor renting is always better, so they compare every cost honestly, including repairs, taxes and the cost of moving.
Marta learns that insurance protects a plan against large shocks. She and Dev check that they have the basic cover that they need, and nothing that they do not.
After her course, Marta receives a promotion and a pay rise. She decides to send most of the extra money into her plan before it can change her lifestyle.
Marta goes through all her charges once a year, including fund fees and account fees. Small percentages repeat every year, and they can take a large part of her growth.
Marta remembers that prices rise over time, which is called inflation. Her plan has to grow faster than prices, so she updates her yearly costs every year.
Marta and Dev sit down and combine their money plans into a single page. They talk about the things that they both want, and they agree on their goals together.
Six years after she began, Marta's savings reach the size of a full year of her costs. It is a big milestone, and she and Dev celebrate with a small dinner.
As her savings grow, work begins to feel more like a choice and less like a need. Marta asks the depot if she can work four days a week.
Marta spends time thinking about what enough looks like for her. A clear idea of enough protects her from chasing more and more without ever feeling satisfied.
Marta realises that her money now has three jobs. Some pays for this year, some is the safe cushion, and the rest is the long-term fund that grows for later.
Marta learns how people spend their savings later in life. They sell a small part each year, keep a cash buffer for bad years, and stay flexible about how much they spend.
Marta finds that tax in later life can be complicated, and that it differs from country to country. For that, she might pay a fee-only adviser for a one-time check.
Kofi gets his first job, and Marta teaches him her plan on a single page. He begins to save from his first paycheque, and he is already ten years ahead of her.
Over ten years, Marta's plan has grown to seven short lines. It has changed a little, but it still fits on a single page, and it still works.
Marta lists the five things that can break a plan: expensive debt, panic selling, high fees, rising spending and needless complexity. She checks them every year like a pilot checking a cockpit.
After ten years, Marta's cushion is strong, her fund has grown, and her habits are firmly in place. The bigger change, though, is that she no longer lies awake at night.
Marta understands now that her wealth was not built by luck or secrets. It came from plain steps, repeated for years, and anyone can begin them tonight.
One simple plan, followed with patience for many years, can build real wealth. This book is general information and not financial advice, so check your own situation or ask a qualified adviser.
C1C2: Marta was thirty-eight, and she spent her days driving a van full of other people's parcels through narrow streets and tall buildings. She earned a steady wage and paid her bills, yet she had no plan whatsoever for her money, and in the quiet hours of the night that gap felt enormous. She decided, at last, that worrying was not a strategy, and that it was time to replace it with a plan.

Over dinner one evening, her younger brother Kofi, who was studying at a university across the city, asked her a question that seemed simple but turned out to be hard. What does it actually mean to be wealthy, he wondered, and how does an ordinary person get there? Marta opened her mouth, closed it again, and admitted that she had never thought about it properly.

They worked it out together over a second cup of coffee, and the answer was surprising. Wealth, it turned out, is not the size of a wage or the polish of a car, but the amount of valuable things that you own once everything that you owe has been subtracted. A person on a modest income can be wealthy, and a person on a very high one can be poor.

Kofi, who liked pictures, drew three interlocking wheels on a napkin and named them earning, keeping and growing. Each wheel drives the next, he said, because what you earn is only useful if you keep some of it, and what you keep is only useful if it is put somewhere that can grow. Marta looked at the napkin and felt, for the first time in months, that the problem had a shape.

Marta announced that her plan would have to fit on one page, with a handful of clear steps and no complicated words. She knew herself well: if it turned into a thick folder of rules, it would end up in a drawer and be forgotten by Friday. Simple things, she said to Kofi, are the only things that survive a busy life.

The first step on her page read, know your numbers, and she took it literally, spreading every bill, statement and letter across the living-room floor like a map. She wrote down what she earned, what she spent, what she owned and what she owed, and the figures were less frightening than the vague fear that had been hiding behind them. Facts, she found, are kinder than fog, and a clear list of numbers can calm a restless mind.

When Marta subtracted everything she owed from everything she owned, the result was her net worth, and it was a small figure that made her cheeks burn for a moment. She reminded herself that every journey has a starting point, and that a true number, however modest, is a far better foundation than a flattering guess. She wrote it at the top of the page with a firm pen, and she did not look away from it.

Next she added up what her ordinary life cost each month, including rent, food, fuel, bills and the occasional treat, and then multiplied the total by twelve. This yearly cost, she realised, was the most important number on the page, because everything that followed would be measured against it. A plan for wealth, it seemed, begins with knowing exactly how much living costs.

The second step was the one that everybody knows and few people follow: spend less than you earn. The gap between the money coming in and the money going out, Marta saw, was the engine of the entire plan, because without a gap there was nothing to keep and nothing to grow. Everything else on her page depended on making that gap wide enough, and on keeping it wide for many years.

Looking down her list, Marta noticed that three items towered over all the rest: her housing, her transport and her food, which together swallowed the majority of her wage. Small daily savings were pleasant, but these three were where real change would be found, and she resolved to look at them first. It is easier, she thought, to move one mountain than to sweep away a thousand pebbles.

Marta talked it over with her partner Dev, a school cook with a calm temperament, and together they decided to move to a smaller flat that was cheaper and closer to her depot. It was an inconvenience for one weekend and a saving for years, and it reduced her biggest cost more than any number of cancelled subscriptions could have done. She felt as though she had paid herself a rise, and nobody at the depot had needed to approve it.

The third step on her page was to clear any expensive debt, for interest at a high rate is a force that works against a saver every single day. Marta still carried a credit card balance from a difficult year, and each month the interest took a bite out of her progress, like a leak in the bottom of a bucket. She made a plan to pay it off, and she did not touch the card again.

After nine months of steady and rather dull payments, the credit card balance reached zero, and Marta felt a lightness that she had not experienced in years. She wrote a small rule on her page: that expensive debt must go first, whereas a cheap, sensible loan could be kept and repaid on schedule. The point, she told Kofi, was not to hate all debt, but to refuse the kind that bites.

The fourth step was a cushion, a reserve of money set aside to meet life's surprises, which in her case meant a van repair, a lost shift or a sudden illness. She aimed for three to six months of her ordinary costs, because that sum would let her face a bad month without borrowing, and without panic. A surprise was only a disaster, she realised, if she had nothing to meet it with.

Marta placed her cushion in a safe, simple savings account that she could reach within a day, and she kept it well away from anything that rose and fell with the markets. Money meant for emergencies, she reasoned, should never depend on a good week on the stock exchange, since emergencies are not polite enough to wait for one. It earned only a little interest, but its job was safety rather than growth, and it performed that job very well.

The fifth step was the one that made her most nervous: growing her savings by putting them into a single broad, low-cost fund that held hundreds of companies at the same time. Because her money would be spread across a large slice of the economy, no single failure could ruin her, and the low cost would leave more of the growth in her own pocket. She read the details three times before she dared to begin, and then she pressed the button with a trembling finger.

There were hundreds of funds to choose from, and each one came with a glossy brochure, but Marta decided that a single plain fund was far better than a dozen clever ones. Every extra choice is another chance to make a mistake or to pay a fee, she reasoned, and a plan with fewer parts also has fewer ways of breaking. She found that she slept better with one decision than with twelve, and her notebook became a good deal shorter.

Kofi, who had studied a little economics, advised her to ask anyone who offered financial advice a very simple question: how are you paid? Complicated products, he warned, often reward the person selling them far more than the person buying them, and an honest adviser will always answer plainly. Marta wrote the question on a small card and kept it in her wallet.

Over long periods, stock markets in many countries have tended to rise, but the road has never been smooth, and it is marked by sudden falls that arrive without warning. Nobody can say when the next one will come or how long it will last, and the past offers no promises about the future. Marta understood that the price of the possible growth was the willingness to sit through the bumps.

Marta wrote a short rule on a card and fixed it to her refrigerator with a magnet: in a bad year, do not sell in a panic, and do not watch the prices every day. She knew that her own fear was the greatest threat to her plan, far greater than any crash, and that a rule written in a calm moment is a gift to the frightened person she might later become. The card never moved from the door, and it was read more often than any letter she received.

The sixth step was automation, and Marta arranged that on the day after each payday, a fixed amount would travel by itself into her cushion and into her fund. She no longer had to remember, to feel brave, or to resist a tempting sale, because the plan simply happened in the background like a clock. The best plans, she was beginning to think, are the ones that need no heroes.

Kofi pointed out that, among all the numbers on her page, the one with the greatest power was her savings rate, which is the share of her income that she kept. The higher that share, the sooner a person can stop depending on a wage, and the lower her costs, the smaller the pile she will need in the first place. It works from both ends at once, he said, like a bridge that is built from both banks of a river.

How large a pile of savings would she eventually need to feel free, Marta wondered, and was there any way of finding out? Some planners use a rule of thumb that about twenty-five times yearly costs may support spending for several decades, because it lets a person use about four percent of the pile each year. It is only a rough guide and carries no guarantee, but it gave her a target to aim at, and a target is worth having.

As an example, suppose that her life cost 24,000 a year; twenty-five times that figure is 600,000, which looked like a mountain on the notepad but which could be climbed in careful steps over many years. The rule is only a guide, and real life brings changes in costs, prices and returns, so it must be checked again and again. Still, a number gave the dream a firm outline, and a dream with an outline is far easier to pursue.

Marta noticed an elegant consequence of the rule: if she could lower her yearly costs by 1,000, her target pile would shrink by about 25,000, and the saved money could go into the fund as well. Cutting a cost was therefore a double victory, since it moved her toward the target and made the target smaller at the same time. Every small saving, she saw, was working twice, and she began to look for them with real enthusiasm.

Saving is only one half of the picture, Kofi reminded her, since there is a limit to how far costs can fall but almost no limit to how far income can rise. Marta enrolled in a night course in logistics, hoping that it might lead to a better job at the depot, and she accepted extra shifts when they suited her. Each extra coin earned was a coin that could be sent into the plan.

In many countries, governments and employers offer special retirement accounts that shelter savings from some tax or that add extra money whenever the worker contributes, and these deals are worth finding. Marta visited the personnel office at the depot and discovered a scheme with a modest employer match that she had never noticed before. Rules vary widely from place to place, so she wrote down the details with care.

One year after she wrote her plan, Marta sat down with the page and checked each line in turn: the cushion was full, the credit card was gone, and the first small growth had appeared in her fund. None of it felt dramatic, but when she compared her net worth with that first number, the difference was undeniable. A plan that works quietly, she decided, is still working, and she did not need applause to prove it.

In the second year, her old van broke down on a wet motorway, and the garage returned a bill that would once have sent her into a frightened spiral of borrowing. Instead, she paid it from the cushion in a single calm payment, and then began quietly to refill the reserve. It was exactly the situation that the cushion had been created to meet, and it worked.

In the third year, the news was full of falling markets, and the value of her fund dropped by about a fifth in a few weeks, just as her planning had warned it might. She read the card on her refrigerator, breathed deeply, and did absolutely nothing except continue her automatic payments, which were now buying more for the same money. It was the hardest and most important thing that she did all year, and nobody was there to applaud her for it.

In time, prices recovered, although nobody could have predicted the date, and Marta saw her fund climb back past its earlier level. Recoveries do not always arrive so quickly, and no one can promise them, but she had learned that her real task was not to outwit the market but to remain in her seat until it moved. Patience, she thought, had turned out to be her most valuable skill, and it was one that cost nothing at all.

Kofi's friend had put most of his savings into a fashionable new idea that everyone at his college was discussing, and within a few months he had lost a large part of it. Marta felt sorry for him, and she also felt a quiet gratitude that her own plan was plain and unexciting. Boredom, she told Kofi, is an underrated virtue in the world of money, and excitement is often the most expensive feeling there is.

After a few years, Marta and Dev began to think about buying a home of their own, and they discovered that the question has no single right answer. Buying brings repairs, taxes, insurance and the cost of moving, whereas renting brings flexibility and a landlord, so the sensible thing is to compare every cost honestly in your own town. They made a list of every cost, and they took their time, because a home is far too large a decision to hurry.

Insurance, Marta learned, is the guard at the gate of a plan, since one serious illness or accident can destroy years of careful saving. She and Dev compared policies, made certain that they had the basic cover that their situation demanded, and declined the glossy extras that they did not. The exact products differ by country, so she asked a trusted adviser to explain the local rules.

When her course ended, Marta was promoted to a position at the depot, and the new wage was a small but welcome improvement. She decided to send the greater part of the extra pay straight into the plan before it could be absorbed by a larger flat or a shinier car. Her life would improve, but gently, and her future would improve a great deal more, which seemed to her a good trade.

Once a year, Marta went through every charge attached to her accounts, from the fund's annual fee to the platform's account fee, because small percentages repeat every year and can consume a surprising part of the growth. She switched to a cheaper platform when she found one, and the change cost her an afternoon and saved her money for decades. Vigilance about costs, she decided, was the most profitable hobby she had ever had.

Marta remembered that prices tend to rise over the years, and that her target number was therefore not fixed but would grow along with the cost of living. Every year she updated her yearly costs and her target, and she noted with approval that a fund of companies has often grown faster than prices over long periods, even though it makes no promises. Cash alone, she knew, would lose power while she watched, and so growth had to be part of the plan.

Marta and Dev sat down at the kitchen table one evening and merged their separate habits into a single plan, because two people who hide their money from each other make one another's lives harder. They talked about what each of them wanted, from a small garden to a long journey, and discovered that their goals were more alike than either had guessed. A shared plan, Marta said, is a stronger plan, and she felt closer to Dev than ever before.

Six years after writing her first page, Marta looked at her accounts and realised that her savings now equalled a full year of her costs, which was a milestone that she had once thought impossible. She and Dev celebrated with a modest dinner, and Kofi, now a graduate, raised a glass of water in her honour. The mountain was still ahead of her, but she was on it, and moving.

As her savings grew, Marta noticed a change in how she thought about her job, for work was gradually becoming something that she chose rather than something that she could not do without. She asked the depot whether she could work four days a week, accepted a slightly lower wage, and spent the extra day with Dev and with a book. That freedom, she said, was the true return on her plan, and no statement could ever display it in a table.

Marta spent an evening asking herself what enough would look like in her own life, and she wrote the answer down in plain words: a small home, good food, travel once a year, and time to read. A clear picture of enough, she realised, protects a person from the endless pursuit of more, because without it no sum can ever feel sufficient. Beyond that line, any additional money would be a choice, a luxury to be enjoyed or given away, and not a need to be chased.

Marta now thought of her money as being divided into three jobs: the part that paid for this year, the cushion that guarded against surprises, and the long-term fund that was growing for the distant future. Each part lived in a different place with a different level of risk, and none of them was asked to do another's work. This separation made the whole plan easier to understand and to trust, and it prevented any one job from being starved.

Marta also studied how people spend savings in later life, and she learned that a common method is to sell a small part of the fund each year and keep a cash buffer for lean years. Flexibility matters a great deal, because a person who can spend a little less in a bad year gives the pile a much better chance of lasting. No rule, she noted, removes the need for judgement, and no rule can foresee the future.

Tax in later life, Marta discovered, can be very complicated and depends heavily on the country, the type of account and the person's age. For this stage, she decided it would be sensible to pay a qualified adviser, preferably one who charged a flat fee rather than earning commissions, to review her plan once and check that nothing had been overlooked. Asking an expert for a specific answer, she thought, is wiser than guessing, and a single fee was a small price for certainty.

When Kofi took his first job, Marta sat him down on a park bench and explained her plan from the beginning, one step at a time, on a single sheet of paper. He started saving from his very first pay cheque, and she smiled to realise that he was beginning at an age when she had not yet made a single plan. The habit of simple steps, it seemed, could be handed on, like a good recipe or an old and well-worn tool.

Over ten years, her plan had grown from six lines to seven, with a new line about insurance, but it still fitted comfortably on a single sheet and could be read in less than a minute. She was pleased to notice that the more she understood about money, the less she wished to complicate it. Wisdom, it seemed, sometimes shows itself in the choice to keep things plain, and she was glad to have chosen it.

Looking back, Marta wrote down the five things that most often break a plan like hers: expensive debt, panic selling, high fees, spending that rises with income, and needless complexity. She checked them once a year, the way a pilot checks a cockpit, knowing that most disasters begin with a small neglected item. Prevention, she thought, is far cheaper than repair, and a yearly check takes only an evening and a cup of tea.

After ten years, the numbers were impressive in their quiet way: the cushion was solid, the fund had grown through good years and bad ones, and her habits were firmly rooted. The greater change was invisible, because she no longer lay awake worrying, and she felt for the first time that she was steering her life instead of being carried by it. Her page had done what she had hoped, and it had asked for nothing more than patience, honesty and a pen.

Marta understood at last that her progress had not come from luck, or secret knowledge, or an unusual gift, but from a handful of plain steps repeated patiently for years. Anyone with a regular income and a little discipline can begin the same journey, she told her family, even tonight, with a pen and a single sheet of paper. The first step, she added, is simply to know your numbers, and the second is not to be afraid of them.

One simple plan, written on a single page and followed with patience for many years, can build a wealth that is both modest and real, and it can bring peace of mind as well. This book is general information and not financial advice, and no plan can promise any particular result, so anyone with a specific question should consult a qualified adviser. Marta folded her page, smiled, and set off for work, with the whole day and the long road ahead of her.
